# IronGall v1 test vectors

Files any IronGall implementation can check itself against, made with stock tools only (`generate.sh`: bash, od, base64, sha256sum, ssh-keygen, and age ≥ 1.3 for the one ciphertext). Every vector is judged at the time in `now`.

**The keys are public test keys**, all of RFC 8032 §7.1 (`input/*.ed25519`: the seed, then the public key, in hex): box A's identity is TEST 1 and box B's is TEST 2; A's working key is TEST 3, B's is TEST 1024, and a second working key of A's is TEST SHA(abc). The age recipients in `input/` are public keys whose secret keys were discarded, so nothing here decrypts.

| Path | What | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `a/`, `b/` | each box's `identity.doc` and `address`; `work-cert.pub`, its identity's certificate for its working key; its prekey statements `prekey-<serial>.txt` with `.sig`, signed by the working key; A's `revoke.txt` with `revoke.sig`, signed by the identity itself; and A's `pass.txt`, `pass.sig` and `pass.authorization`, a pass for a server it calls `irongall.example` | all valid. `a/prekey-1` is post-quantum, `a/prekey-2` X25519 only (`--no-pq`); `a/prekey-1.txt.sha256.sig` signs with SHA-256 instead of SHA-512, which verifiers accept. The pass runs out ten minutes after `now` |
| `cert/bad-*` | a certificate (`.pub`) that breaks one rule, and a signature made under it (`.sig`) over `a/prekey-1.txt` in A's prekey namespace | every one refused for box A. The signature is good under the certificate it carries: the certificate is what fails. `ssh-keygen -Y verify` alone takes `bad-extensions`, `bad-key-id` and `bad-serial-zero` |
| `message/` | `a-to-b.line`, an envelope from A to B as its one line; `a-to-b.sig`, A's working key's signature over it for B; `a-to-b.plain`, what is encrypted (the line, the signature, the padding); `a-to-b.age`, that encrypted to B's prekey | the line and the signature are what a client makes from the same keys, byte for byte; the age file is a whole number of blocks |
| `plain/accept-*`, `refuse-*` | what box B decrypts | delivered or refused, as named, with these codes: `refuse-no-line-feed`, `-no-signature`, `-blank-line-before-the-signature`, `-signature-first`, `-no-end-line`, `-end-line-without-its-line-feed`, `-crlf` and `-envelope-on-two-lines` as `bad_message`; `refuse-no-identity`, `-identity-not-base64` and `-identity-of-small-order` as `bad_identity`; `refuse-signed-for-another-box`, `-signed-by-the-identity`, `-signed-by-a-bare-working-key`, `-certificate-ended`, `-line-changed-after-signing` and `-another-box-s-identity-document` as `bad_signature`; `refuse-from-is-not-the-identity` and `-to-another-box` as `reattributed`. In `accept-anything-after-the-signature` a second envelope, signed by B, follows the first END line and is never read. `refuse-another-box-s-identity-document` is the forgery an identity member invites: A's document beside a certificate B's identity signed |
| `identity/*.doc` | malformed identity documents, and well-formed ones holding a small-order or non-canonical Ed25519 key | every one rejected |
| `prekey/bad-*` | prekey statements with a `.sig` by A's working key, in A's namespace, except where the name says otherwise | every one rejected. `bad-outlives-its-certificate` is signed under the certificate beside it, which ends in ten days |
| `prekey/expired` | a valid statement whose `not_after` is `now` | valid, but expired: a sender must not encrypt to it |
| `prekey/too-long` | a valid statement valid for 33 days and one second | not expired, but a server must refuse to publish it |
| `envelope/accept-*`, `refuse-*` | envelopes of a message whose signature by A verified, received by B | accepted or refused, as named. Keys match exactly and none may appear twice, so every reader takes the same values: in `accept-case-variant-key` the body is `"benign"` (`BODY` is an unknown key, ignored); `refuse-duplicate-key` has two `from`s; `refuse-version-string` has `"v":"1"`, which is not the number 1; `refuse-not-utf8` and `refuse-two-objects` are not one UTF-8 JSON object. Strict on what a loose reader lets through: `refuse-msg-id-newline` ends its `msg_id` with a newline, `refuse-subject-number` has a number where a string goes, and `refuse-sent-at-second-60` names a second some date parsers carry into the next minute |

Ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so an implementation that signs these statements with these keys, under these certificates, must produce byte-identical `.sig` files. A certificate is made once and kept, since `ssh-keygen` puts a random nonce in one, and so is `message/a-to-b.age`, since age encryption is randomised; everything else regenerates byte for byte.
